newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 5.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Feb 5.

text.p: THE DOMINION

Chief District Court Judge Ron Young said on Tuesday that the conviction of former judge Robert Hesketh for fraud shamed him and was a blow to the district court's image. But it confirmed that no one was above the law, Judge Young said. He was commenting after the sentencing of Hesketh in the High Court at Auckland yesterday. "The community has a right to expect that those who sit in judgment upon others are beyond reproach," he said. Page 1.

A fresh investigation is being carried out into Aotearoa Television Network after claims of lavish spending on clothes by NZ First MP Tuku Morgan and another of the company's founding directors. Chief executive Puhi Rangiaho and director Tawini Rangihau have said they have called in accountants Spicer and Oppenheim to go through the company accounts. Page 1.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger on Tuesday defended beleaguered Maori TV company Aotearoa Television Network, saying it had delivered more programming than it was funded for, and questioning whether the government should be concerned with the comapany's structure. It is understood senior Cabinet ministers are likely to decide late today whether to proceed with the $4 million the station needs to continue after tomorrow (Thursday). Page 2.

The minister responsible for the National Library, Wyatt Creech, has refused to issue publicly documents showing how the library spent almost $9 million on a computer project now terminated. Creech turned down a request under the Official Information Act from The Dominion for copies of the briefings made to Cabinet from the National Library, the Treasury, and the State Services Commission about the library's national document information system project. Page 2.

New Zealand was still seeking an undertaking from the owners of a ship carrying nuclear waste to Japan that it would not breach New Zealand's exclusive economic zone when it passed through the Tasman Sea, Foreign Minister Don McKinnon said on Tuesday. Page 2.

The high dollar cost New Zealand more than $2 billion last year, according to Labour finance spokesman Michael Cullen. Dr Cullen based his claim on a graph of exports between 1987 and 1996. The graph shows exports rising fairly steadily between March 1987 and March 1995, but then levelling off. Page 2.

The sharemarket plunged 38 points on Tuesday led by a dramatic 23-cent fall in Telecom. The NZSE 40 capital index closed 1.6 percent down at 2339.94 on high turnover of $74.46 million and has now fallen 100 points since January 20. Telecom's fall saw it close on $7.09, with more than 3 million shares traded. Most of the market leaders tapered off in active trading. Brokers said it had been a long time since the main index had suffered a correction of such magnitude. Page 20.

The Commerce Commission yesterday gave a preliminary thumbs-down to a bid by the Airways Corporation to shield itself from competition for the next year. The corporation had asked for authorisation to continue using a cross-subsidy system for the air traffic control service charges. Airways uses profits from its monopolistic serves to cross-subsidise contestable services, but plans to change to a system reflecting the cost of each service. Page 20.

First NZ Captial and BZW had been appointed for Telecom's share buyback, Telecom said on Tuesday. The buyback would begin soon after third quarter results were announced on February 18, Telecom said. Telecom is to buy back $1 billion of shares, half of them from major shareholders Bell Atlantic and Ameritech. Page 20.

Plastics manufacturer PDL Industries on Tuesday reported a $9.4 million bottom-line profit in the nine months to December 31, down six percent from the $10.04 million last year. The result was on sales revenue of $252.8 million in the nine months, $172.59 million of which was sourced from New Zealand, $56.33 million from overseas operations and $23.89 million from New Zealand exports. Page 20.

Market confirmation that Nestle plans to make an assault on the New Zealand icecream market could be a deliberate tactic to scare off rival bidders for Tip Top, sources close to Tip Top said on Tuesday. Nestle is one of several bidders that are understood to have looked at the books of Tip Top, which has been put up for sale by owners Heinz Wattie. Page 20.

Irish newspaper magnate Tony O'Reilly's personal direct stake in Wilson and Horton will end this month after a share mop-up. Shares in Wilson and Horton bought by Dublin-based Independent Newspapers and family interests of Dr O'Reilly prior to a takeover bid are being transferred to Independent Press Communications. This will complete a deal announced to shareholders at the time of the takeover bid by Independent Newspapers last September, but delayed till now while fine detail of the deal was raked over. Page 20.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

Senior cabinet ministers are under intense pressure to make up their minds on Wednesday whether to reinstate the cash lifeline for Aotearoa Television, with funding for the channel drying up within 48 hours and the political mess threatening to cloud Waitangi Day. The Ministry of Commerce has so far given the Aotearoa Television Network the all-clear, advising ministers that its investigations show public money was spend properly on the programming that the fledging Maori language channel contracted to provide.

Revelations of a $16,000 menswear spending spree by Aotearoa Television directors and staff had the Maori channel's management reeling again on Tuesday night. The besieged company denied approving such spending and said it has now commissioned a full audit of its own books.

Telecom will be at pains not to be a market-maker when it begins its $1 billion share buyback programme shortly after the release of its third-quarter result on February 18. An explanatory document being seen to shareholders outlines the
procedural safeguards it has adopted. Based on a United States experience, they are designed to prevent a company from using buybacks to manipulate the market in its shares.

Natural Gas Corporation has been taken to task by Justice Sir Ian Barker for its conduct before and during last year's Kapuni gas trial. In his judgment, Barker said he found it difficult to understand the absense from the witness box of the NGC chief executive, Richard Bentley. No explanation was offered.

Upper Hutt timber company Parapine Timber may be used as a listing vehicle for shipping centre developer ProMall Ltd. Parapine yesterday advised the stock exchange it had acquired at no cost an option to buy a 25 percent stake in ProMall. The Wellington-based ProMall holds all the rights, licences, designs and agreements relating to the New Zealand-wide development of shopping centres known as ProMall.

The Commerce Commission on Tuesday gave a preliminary thumbs-down to a request by Airways Corporation that would allow it to delay competition for air traffic control services at airports until at least March next year. The state-owned corporation's present network pricing system effectively cross-subsidises a potentially contestable service -- air traffic control for take-offs and landings -- from services in which Airways' monopoly is secure, namely air traffic control for the rest of a flight.

Dividing the Kapuni gas reserves will both stimulate competition and encourage exploration, Justice Sir Ian Barker said in Monday's lengthy trial judgment. barker and Australian lay expert Gaire Blunt had "struggled with a mass of evidence and submissions" from the 48-day hearing which finished last August. The plaintiffs, mining companies Shell and Todd Petroleum Mining, were challenging the contract signed with the government in 1987 giving rights to New Zealand's first natural gas field at Kapuni, in Taranaki.

Fletcher Challenge and Natural Gas Corporation last year agreed in principle to buy gas from the Kupe partners, but never signed the deal because of the damage it could do to their pending court action over the Kapuni field. The Kupe field is operated by 40 percent shareholder Western Mining, with listed explorer NZ Oil and Gas holding a 16.5 percent stake. Those companies have reported an imminent deal for Kupe at various times over the last two days.

PDL Holdings has raised its forecast for its March-year tax paid profit from $12.4 million to between $12.5 and $13 million, despite reporting a six percent profit drop to a $9.4 million for the nine months to December 31. The company had previously forecast a $12.4 million profit at its annual meeting in September. Don Sollitt, the executive chairman and chief executive officer of PDL, said on Tuesday the nine month trading was slightly under those projections.

Prudential said on Tuesday its superannuation sales grew in 1996, reflecting a rising public awareness of the need to save for retirement. An increase of more than 50 percent in retail superannuation plan sales to $16.6 million led to an overall 34 percent rise in sales of Prudential products in 1996.

The Reserve Bank's move last year to be explicit about how it measures the trade-off between interest rates and the currency appears to have produced some stability in financial markets, according to an analysis by Bankers Trust. The analysis showed that monetary conditions were unusually stable in

January. The Bankers Trust Monetary Conditions Index, which combines 90-day bank bills and the trade-weighted currency index to produce an overall measure of conditions, averaged 126 in January, up from 123 in December.
